top_choice_rationale: Anne Carson (P002) remains my first choice on public knowledge of the works, which I have not re-read or independently verified. Her voice is highly recognizable. In Autobiography of Red the Geryon material becomes a verse novel about desire and estrangement. In Nox elegy becomes an archival, physical object built around a brother's death. In both, formal invention carries grief, desire and the limits of language rather than standing in for them. Scholarship, translation and poetry read as one practice across decades, so the case does not rest on a single book. I would rest the citation on the original writing (the verse novel, the elegy and the essay-poems) and not on hybridity alone or on translation and scholarship as separate claims. My reservations are real. Her most design-dependent books cannot be fully judged in translation. The corpus is mostly short and fragmentary, which makes the sustained-breadth case harder than for a large architectural oeuvre. I cannot show that her later work matches the best-known books. Cărtărescu (P001) is a close second. He fits a cumulative-architecture standard more naturally, and I could support him on the stated criteria if P002 fails. His citation should rest on the prose project, with the poetry as foundation. The open question is whether his later volumes deepen or repeat the earlier ones. Tawada (P003) is third because her bilingual formal method is serious, but I cannot judge the Japanese and German corpus or whether the later novels develop the method. I rank all three candidates above no award (P000), since each is a substantial oeuvre under the common criteria. Translation uncertainty affects all of them and does not separate them.
